Let $(\mathsf X,\mathcal X,\mu)$ be a measure space. An **unnormalized target density** is a measurable function $\tilde p:\mathsf X\to[0,\infty)$ with
$$Z_p:=\int_{\mathsf X}\tilde p\,d\mu\in(0,\infty).$$
The target probability measure is $\pi(dx)=\tilde p(x)\mu(dx)/Z_p$. A **proposal density** is a measurable $q:\mathsf X\to[0,\infty)$ with $\int q\,d\mu=1$; write $Q(dx)=q(x)\mu(dx)$. The input integrand $f:\mathsf X\to\mathbb R$ is measurable, and the input sample $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ is IID with law $Q$, in the sense of [[def-identically-distributed-and-iid-random-variables]]. The normalizing constant $Z_p$ is known for this algorithm.

**Admissible conditions for an unbiased estimate:** $n\ge1$, $q>0$ $\mu$-almost everywhere on $\{x:f(x)\tilde p(x)\ne0\}$, and the random variable
$$Y:=\begin{cases}f(X_1)\tilde p(X_1)/(Z_pq(X_1)),&q(X_1)>0,\\0,&q(X_1)=0\end{cases}$$
is integrable under $Q$. The support condition makes the value on $q=0$ immaterial to the target integral.

**Well-defined weights:** The reciprocal map $r(s)=1/s$ for $s>0$ and $r(s)=0$ for $s\le0$ is Borel. Its composition with $q$, multiplied by the measurable inputs, makes the piecewise weight and weighted integrand measurable ([[thm-composition-with-borel-functions-preserves-measurability]], [[thm-arithmetic-and-lattice-operations-preserve-measurability]]).

**Procedure and output:** For each supplied draw $X_i$, set $Y_i=f(X_i)\tilde p(X_i)/(Z_pq(X_i))$ when $q(X_i)>0$ and set $Y_i=0$ otherwise. Return
$$\hat\mu_{\mathrm{IS}}:=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nY_i.$$
Separate variance and central limit claims require the corresponding weighted second-moment hypothesis.

Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S,\Sigma)$ be a random element, let
$\mathbb P_X$ be its law, and let $g:(S,\Sigma)\to\mathbb R$ or
$g:(S,\Sigma)\to\mathbb C$ be measurable.

1. If $g\ge0$, then
   $$\mathbb E[g(X)]=\int_S g\,d\mathbb P_X.$$
2. If $g(X)$ is integrable, then $g$ is integrable with respect to
   $\mathbb P_X$ and the same formula holds:
   $$\mathbb E[g(X)]=\int_S g\,d\mathbb P_X.$$

The class $L^1(\mu)$ is a complex vector space, and the Lebesgue integral is
complex-linear on it:
$$\int (\alpha f+\beta g)\,d\mu=\alpha\int f\,d\mu+\beta\int g\,d\mu \qquad(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C,\ f,g\in L^1(\mu)).$$

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space.

- If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, its **expectation** is the
  extended-valued integral
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P\in[0,+\infty].$$
- If $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ or $X:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ is integrable in the sense
  of [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]], its
  **expectation** is again
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P,$$
  now a finite real or complex number.

For an integrable real random variable,
$$\mathbb E[X]=\mathbb E[X^+]-\mathbb E[X^-],$$
where $X^+$ and $X^-$ are its positive and negative parts.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. Then
$$\int g\,d(f\,d\mu)=\int gf\,d\mu.$$

Let $f:X\to\mathbb R$ be measurable. Its positive and negative parts are
$$f^+:=\max\{f,0\},\qquad f^-:=\max\{-f,0\};$$
they are measurable by
[[prop-closure-properties-of-measurable-functions-used-by-the-integral]] and
satisfy $f=f^+-f^-$ and $|f|=f^++f^-$.

The **Lebesgue integral of a real measurable function** is defined whenever at
most one of $\int f^+\,d\mu$ and $\int f^-\,d\mu$ is $+\infty$, in which case
$$\int f\,d\mu:=\int f^+\,d\mu-\int f^-\,d\mu.$$
The function is **integrable** when both integrals are finite, equivalently
when $\int|f|\,d\mu<+\infty$.

For a complex measurable function $h=u+iv$ with
$u=\operatorname{Re}h,\ v=\operatorname{Im}h$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]), define $h$ to be
**integrable** when $|h|$ is integrable, and then define
$$\int h\,d\mu:=\int u\,d\mu+i\int v\,d\mu.$$

Use [F5] with density $r=q$ for integration against $Q$ and with $r=\tilde p/Z_p$ for integration against $\pi$. For every $i$, apply the nonnegative case of [F2] to $|Y_i|$. Since $X_i$ has law $Q$,
$$\mathbb E_Q|Y_i|=\int_{\{q>0\}}\frac{|f(x)|\tilde p(x)}{Z_pq(x)}q(x)\,d\mu(x)=\frac1{Z_p}\int_{\{q>0\}}|f|\tilde p\,d\mu\le\frac1{Z_p}\int_{\mathsf X}|f|\tilde p\,d\mu<\infty.$$
Thus $Y_i$ is $Q$-integrable. For any real measurable $h$ whose absolute integral is finite against $r\,d\mu$, apply [F5] separately to $h^+=\max(h,0)$ and $h^-=\max(-h,0)$: both product integrals are finite because $h^\pm\le|h|$. Subtracting their finite identities yields $\int h\,d(r\,d\mu)=\int hr\,d\mu$, since $(hr)^\pm=h^\pm r$ for $r\ge0$ (with the density convention $0\cdot\infty=0$). The integrable case of [F2] therefore gives
$$\mathbb E_Q[Y_i]=\int_{\{q>0\}}\frac{f(x)\tilde p(x)}{Z_pq(x)}q(x)\,d\mu(x)=\frac1{Z_p}\int_{\{q>0\}}f\tilde p\,d\mu.$$
The support condition makes $f\tilde p=0$ $\mu$-almost everywhere on $\{q=0\}$; hence this last integral equals $Z_p^{-1}\int_{\mathsf X}f\tilde p\,d\mu=\int f\,d\pi=\theta$.
By [F1], $\hat\mu_{\mathrm{IS}}=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^nY_i$. Apply [F3] and step 1.1 to obtain $\mathbb E_Q[\hat\mu_{\mathrm{IS}}]=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n\mathbb E_Q[Y_i]=\theta$.

Let $(\mathsf X,\mathcal X,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $\tilde p\ge0$ and $q\ge0$ be measurable densities with $Z_p=\int\tilde p\,d\mu\in(0,\infty)$ and $\int q\,d\mu=1$, and set $\pi(dx)=\tilde p(x)\mu(dx)/Z_p$ and $Q(dx)=q(x)\mu(dx)$. $$\mathbb E_Q[\hat\mu_{\mathrm{IS}}]=\int f\,d\pi.$$

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be an independent family of random elements
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$. For each $i$, let
$g_i:(S_i,\Sigma_i)\to(T_i,\mathcal T_i)$ be measurable. Then the family
$(g_i\circ X_i)_{i\in I}$ is independent.

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be random elements with the same measurable target $(E,\mathcal E)$. They are **identically distributed** if $\mathbb P(X_i\in B)=\mathbb P(X_j\in B)$ for all $i,j\in I$ and $B\in\mathcal E$, that is, their laws in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]] agree. Independence means mutual independence, not merely pairwise independence. No moment assumption is part of either definition. The empty family satisfies these universal conditions vacuously.

Let $(Y_i)_{i\ge1}$ be a real IID sequence. If $\mathbb E|Y_1|<\infty$ and $\mu=\mathbb E[Y_1]$, then $\mathbb E[\bar Y_n]=\mu$ for every $n\ge1$. If also $\mathbb E[Y_1^2]<\infty$ and $\sigma^2=\operatorname{Var}(Y_1)$, then $\operatorname{Var}(\bar Y_n)=\sigma^2/n$ for every $n\ge1$.

Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S,\Sigma)$ be a random element, let
$\mathbb P_X$ be its law, and let $g:(S,\Sigma)\to\mathbb R$ or
$g:(S,\Sigma)\to\mathbb C$ be measurable.

1. If $g\ge0$, then
   $$\mathbb E[g(X)]=\int_S g\,d\mathbb P_X.$$
2. If $g(X)$ is integrable, then $g$ is integrable with respect to
   $\mathbb P_X$ and the same formula holds:
   $$\mathbb E[g(X)]=\int_S g\,d\mathbb P_X.$$

Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is
  $$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same
probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $(Y_i)_{i\ge1}$ be a real IID sequence with $\mu=\mathbb E[Y_1]$ and $0<\sigma^2:=\operatorname{Var}(Y_1)<\infty$. Then
$$\sqrt n\,(\bar Y_n-\mu)\Rightarrow N(0,\sigma^2).$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space and let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. Then
$$\int f\,d\mu=0 \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad f=0 \text{ almost everywhere.}$$

Assume AC. Define $\gamma(E)=\int_E e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\,dx$ for Borel E in $\mathbb R$. By [[lem-normal-density-has-total-mass-one]] and [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]], gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. [[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]] makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in [[def-dirac-measure]].

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Direct integration gives $\int p=\tfrac12(\int_{-\infty}^0e^x\,dx+\int_0^\infty e^{-x}\,dx)=1$ and $\int q=2\int_0^\infty e^{-2x}\,dx=1$. Also $q(x)>0$ for every $x$, while $f=1$ has target mean $1$ and variance $0$.
Use

By [F5], the ordinary estimate $\bar W_n=n^{-1}\sum_iW_i$ has mean $1$. For each finite $n$, nonnegativity gives $\bar W_n\ge W_1/n$, hence $W_1^2/n^2\le\bar W_n^2$. Monotonicity [F6] and step 2.1 imply $\mathbb E_Q[\bar W_n^2]\ge n^{-2}\mathbb E_Q[W_1^2]=\infty$. If its centered second moment were finite, the inequality $x^2\le2(x-1)^2+2$ would imply $\mathbb E_Q[\bar W_n^2]<\infty$, a contradiction. Thus the centered second moment is infinite, so the estimate does not have finite variance under [F4]. This refutes the sufficiency claim.

citations.quote:
For the nonnegative importance weights $w_1,\ldots,w_n$ in [[alg-self-normalized-importance-sampling]], with $n\ge1$ and at least one positive weight, define the **weight-based effective sample size** by
$$\operatorname{ESS}_w:=\frac{(\sum_{i=1}^nw_i)^2}{\sum_{i=1}^nw_i^2}.$$
It is a diagnostic of observed weight imbalance. It depends only on the weights, not on the integrand, proposal regions that were never sampled, or target mass outside the observed sample. It does not certify support coverage, finite variance, accuracy, or convergence.

Let $(\mathsf X,\mathcal X,\mu)$ be a measure space. The unnormalized target density is a measurable $\tilde p\ge0$ with $0<Z_p=\int\tilde p\,d\mu<\infty$ and target $\pi(dx)=\tilde p(x)\mu(dx)/Z_p$. Let $q\ge0$ be a measurable proposal probability density against $\mu$, let $Q(dx)=q(x)\mu(dx)$, and let $f$ be a measurable real-valued integrand. The input $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ is an IID sample from $Q$ in the sense of [[def-identically-distributed-and-iid-random-variables]], with $n\ge1$. For target interpretation require $q>0$ $\pi$-almost everywhere. Write
$$W_i:=\begin{cases}\tilde p(X_i)/q(X_i),&q(X_i)>0,\\0,&q(X_i)=0.\end{cases}$$
This is a nonnegative unnormalized importance weight; the value on $q=0$ is immaterial under $Q$ and under the stated target support condition.

The reciprocal map that is $1/s$ for $s>0$ and $0$ for $s\le0$ is Borel. Its composition with $q$, multiplied by $\tilde p$, makes $W_i$ measurable by [[thm-composition-with-borel-functions-preserves-measurability]] and [[thm-arithmetic-and-lattice-operations-preserve-measurability]].

**Procedure and output:** Compute $S_n=\sum_{i=1}^nW_i$. If $S_n=0$, return the status **no estimate: zero observed target weight**. If $S_n>0$, return
$$\hat\theta_{\mathrm{SN}}:=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^nW_if(X_i)}{S_n}.$$
For consistency require $\mathbb E_QW_1=Z_p\in(0,\infty)$ and $\mathbb E_Q[W_1|f(X_1)|]<\infty$. A ratio CLT and its Monte Carlo standard error require finite second moments of $W_1$ and $W_1f(X_1)$.

derivations.claim: Let $\mathsf X=\{a,b\}$, $\tilde p(a)=\tilde p(b)=1$, so $Z_p=2$ and $\pi(b)=1/2$. Take proposal masses $q(a)=99/100$ and $q(b)=1/100$. This proposal has full target support, and the event $E_n=\{X_1=\cdots=X_n=a\}$ has probability $(99/100)^n>0$.

On $E_n$, all observed weights equal $W(a)=100/99>0$. By [F1], $\operatorname{ESS}_w=(nW(a))^2/(nW(a)^2)=n$, while no sample is at $b$ and the target assigns $b$ probability $1/2$. Thus the claimed certification fails on an event of positive probability.
